Objective: Track signed charge through transfers and distinguish mobile charge redistribution in conductors from localized polarization or charge in insulators.
No hard prerequisite is declared. Begin with the operational rule that charge is transferred between parts of an isolated system rather than created or destroyed.
Electric charge is signed and conserved. For an isolated system, the algebraic sum of all charges is the same before and after contact, rubbing, or separation.
Electron gain makes an object more negative; electron loss makes it more positive. A neutral object has equal positive and negative charge, not an absence of charged constituents.
In conductors, mobile charges redistribute in response to electric influence. In insulators, charge and polarization are more localized because charges are not free to move through the material.
Use a signed-charge ledger with one row per object. Record transfers as equal and opposite ledger changes, then check the total before interpreting material behavior.
I sum signed charges first and never add magnitudes alone. Then I ask whether the material permits mobile charge to redistribute or keeps the response localized.
Two isolated objects begin neutral. After rubbing, object A has −4 nC. Conservation requires object B to have +4 nC because the isolated pair still totals zero.
A nearby charged rod can rearrange mobile charge in a neutral conductor without changing the conductor’s total charge.
Guided practice: enter every signed charge in the conservation ledger before selecting a final state.
Less support: infer electron transfer direction from the sign change.
Independent practice: distinguish redistribution from localized response in a fresh material case.
Boundary: polarization can separate positive and negative regions while leaving total charge unchanged. Separation of charge is not creation of net charge.

Objective: Use Coulomb’s law to predict force magnitude scaling and attraction or repulsion direction for point-charge pairs.
The charge ledger supplies signed source charges. Coulomb’s law now converts those signs, magnitudes, and separation into a pairwise force.
For point charges, force magnitude is F = k|q1q2|/r². Charge magnitudes multiply, while distance enters through an inverse square.
Like signs repel and opposite signs attract along the line joining the charges. The sign choice determines direction, not a negative force magnitude.
Each charge exerts a force of equal magnitude and opposite direction on the other, even when their charge magnitudes differ.
Split every problem into magnitude and direction columns. Scale |q1q2|/r² for magnitude, then use the sign pair and line of centers for direction.
I calculate a positive magnitude from absolute values and handle direction separately. For comparisons, I use ratios so constants cancel and inverse-square changes remain visible.
If one charge doubles while distance and the other charge stay fixed, |q1q2| doubles and the force magnitude doubles.
If separation doubles, r² grows by four and the force magnitude becomes one-fourth.
Guided practice: separate sign-based direction from magnitude scaling.
Less support: use a force ratio when only one variable changes.
Independent practice: combine charge and distance scaling in one comparison.
Boundary: unequal charges do not exert unequal pair-force magnitudes on each other. Newton’s third-law pair remains equal and opposite.

Objective: Interpret electric-field direction, magnitude, field lines, and vector superposition for bounded point-charge and uniform-field configurations.
Coulomb’s law described force between a source and a second charge. Electric field separates the source-created condition from the test charge used to probe it.
Electric field is force per positive test charge, E = F/qtest. Its direction is the force direction a positive test charge would experience.
Field points away from positive source charge and toward negative source charge. Multiple source fields combine by vector superposition.

Field lines are tangent to field direction, are denser where the represented field is stronger, and do not cross. A bounded parallel-plate region can be treated as approximately uniform away from edges.
At the observation point, draw one vector from each source using positive-test-charge direction, then add components. Keep source field separate from the sign of any later test charge.
I place a hypothetical positive test charge at the point, draw each source contribution, and only then add vectors. If the actual particle is negative, its force reverses relative to the field.
At the midpoint between equal positive charges, each source field points away from its source. The two vectors have equal magnitude and opposite direction, so the net field is zero.
At the midpoint between equal opposite charges, both source fields point from the positive side toward the negative side, so they add.
Guided practice: use a positive test charge to establish each field-vector direction.
Less support: combine collinear field contributions at a symmetry point.
Independent practice: distinguish field direction from force on a negative particle.
Boundary: zero electric field at a point does not require zero electric potential there; vector cancellation and scalar cancellation follow different rules.

Objective: Use electric potential as a scalar and electrostatic energy U = qV to compare point-charge and equipotential configurations.
The field describes vector force per charge. Potential provides a scalar energy-per-charge representation of the same electrostatic source configuration.
Electric potential is scalar. For point sources, contributions such as kq/r add algebraically with source-charge signs rather than as vectors.
Electrostatic potential energy for a charge at a point is U = qV. A positive charge follows potential sign directly; a negative charge reverses the sign relation.
The electric field points toward decreasing potential. Motion along one equipotential has zero potential difference and requires no electrostatic work.
Keep three rows: source-created V, placed charge q, resulting U = qV. For changes, use ΔU = qΔV and Wfield = −ΔU.
I add potential contributions as signed scalars first. Only after finding V or ΔV do I multiply by the placed charge and decide energy or work direction.
Equal +q and −q sources contribute equal and opposite potentials at their midpoint, so V = 0 there even though their field vectors add.
If a +2 C charge moves through ΔV = −3 V, then ΔU = qΔV = −6 J and the electric field does +6 J of work.
Guided practice: add source potentials algebraically before introducing the placed charge.
Less support: use equipotential and energy relations in a fresh geometry.
Independent practice: track the sign of q when converting potential change to energy change.
Boundary: electric potential can be zero while electric field is nonzero because potential is scalar and field is vector.
